final_task_tree.title: Research compliance across 50 states
final_task_tree.description: We're shipping a consumer mobile app that scans a user's face to verify identity at signup, and we charge a monthly subscription. Before launch I need to know, state by state, which biometric privacy laws apply to us, what notice and written consent we have to collect, how long we're allowed to retain the scan, whether there's a private right of action, and what the penalties are. Flag the states that are genuinely dangerous to launch in.

comments.body:
Starting. Scoping this as five research strands:

1. **Tier 1 — dedicated biometric statutes with teeth** (IL BIPA, TX CUBI, WA HB 1493) — these drive the whole compliance design.
2. **Tier 2 — comprehensive state privacy laws treating biometrics as sensitive data** (CA/CO/CT/VA/OR/TX + the 15-ish others now in force) — opt-in consent for sensitive data, no private right of action except CA breach.
3. **Tier 3 — sector/adjacent laws** that catch face scans (NYC biometric identifier ordinance, Portland OR face recognition ban, CO/IL AI acts, BIPA copycats in other cities).
4. **The subscription angle** — this is a separate legal exposure the brief implies but doesn't name: FTC ROSCA + the state auto-renewal laws. Charging monthly recurring is its own private-right-of-action magnet in CA.
5. **Synthesis** — the state-by-state matrix + a launch risk ranking.

One scoping note I want to flag up front rather than bury: a truly *complete* 50-state matrix is a licensed-attorney deliverable, and the honest version of this research is that ~30 states have no biometric-specific rule that changes what you build. I'm going to produce a matrix that names every state, but the substance will be concentrated in the ~20 that actually change your product decisions. I'll be explicit about which cells are "researched and verified" vs "no specific law found."
comments.author: agent

comments.body:
**Done — report attached. Six research subtasks closed, eight action subtasks open for you.**

**The four things that actually matter:**

1. **Illinois BIPA** is the reason to build the strict flow. Private right of action, no injury required, 5-year limitations period, fee-shifting. The 2024 SB 2979 amendment capped per-user recovery but did nothing for per-class exposure.
2. **Texas** has no private right of action and is still Tier 1 — the AG got **$1.4B** from Meta over face-tagging and treats collection *and* storage as separate violations. Also: TRAIGA's new AI-training exemption (eff. 1 Jan 2026) explicitly does **not** help us, because it excludes systems used to uniquely identify individuals. That's us.
3. **Portland, Oregon** is the finding I'd have missed with a state-level-only search. $1,000 **per day**, private right of action. Exposure scales with elapsed time, not user count — so a small, long-running violation is expensive.
4. **Washington's risk isn't the biometric statute.** RCW 19.375 excludes photographs and "data generated therefrom," so it likely doesn't reach us. The **My Health My Data Act** — broad private right of action — might.

**Two things I added that weren't in the brief.** You asked about biometrics; the monthly subscription is a second, independent class-action surface (California ARL as amended by AB 2863, in force since July 2025), so I researched it as its own strand. And I flagged the *bundling* trap: putting biometric consent and subscription consent in one checkbox can fail BIPA's standalone-release requirement and the ARL's affirmative-consent requirement simultaneously. Easy to get wrong, easy to avoid.

**Best single risk reduction:** go ephemeral on the template. If you never store it, BIPA retention exposure approaches zero, Texas is trivially met, Maryland's "strictly necessary" test is easy, and a breach can't leak biometrics. That's the first decision task and it gates the consent copy, so it needs answering before design starts.

**Three honest limitations:**
- I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice. Three questions need a written opinion and I've written them out verbatim in the counsel task so you can forward it as-is.
- The matrix names all 50 states but the depth is uneven by design — I went deep on the ~20 that change your product and verified absence of a biometric consent statute in the rest rather than auditing each state's UDAP law. Section 8 of the report says so plainly.
- Massachusetts and New York both have pending BIPA-style bills with private rights of action. If NY passes one, this analysis needs revisiting — hence the quarterly check task.

**No answer needed from me to proceed.** Setting the parent to `needs_review`; it stays open because eight children are unstarted. The two decision tasks are the critical path.

report.markdown:
# Biometric & Subscription Compliance — 50-State Launch Assessment

**Product:** consumer mobile app, face scan for identity verification at signup, monthly subscription.
**Date of research:** 5 August 2026.
**Status:** research complete; four decisions and one counsel engagement are open.

> **Read this first.** This is engineering-grade research, not legal advice, and I am not a lawyer. Three questions in here genuinely cannot be closed without a licensed attorney and they are broken out as their own task. Everything else is actionable now.

---

## 1. The short answer

Four things drive almost all of your risk:

1. **Illinois BIPA** is the only law in the country where a plaintiff's lawyer can build a class action out of a *paperwork* failure, with no injury required. It is the reason to build the strict flow.
2. **Texas** has no private right of action but has an Attorney General who extracted **$1.4 billion** from Meta over face-tagging. AG-only enforcement is not the same as low risk.
3. **Portland, Oregon** is the most under-rated item on this list: **$1,000 per day**, private right of action, exposure scaling with *time* rather than user count.
4. **Your subscription is a second, independent class-action surface.** It was not in the brief. California's ARL is strict, in force, and routinely litigated through the UCL.

The good news: **there is no state where compliance is impossible.** Build one national flow to the strictest standard on each axis and the 50-state problem mostly dissolves.

---

## 2. Danger ranking

### 🔴 Tier 1 — genuinely dangerous

| State | Why | Worst case |
|---|---|---|
| **Illinois** | BIPA. Private right of action, no injury required (*Rosenbach*), 5-year SoL (*Tims*), fee-shifting | $1,000 negligent / $5,000 intentional **per person**, + fees |
| **Texas** | CUBI. AG-exclusive but extremely active; AG treats collection *and* storage as separate violations | $25,000/violation, doubling to $50k on the AG's theory |
| **Portland, OR** *(city)* | Private-sector face recognition ban, private right of action | **$1,000 per day**, + fees |
| **Washington** | *Not* the biometric statute — the **My Health My Data Act**, broad private right of action. Applicability to identity-only face scans is unresolved | CPA remedies; no statutory damages, so actual damages must be pleaded |

### 🟠 Tier 2 — strict, manageable, no private right of action for consent failures

**California** (CCPA/CPRA — biometrics are sensitive PI; **breach** is privately actionable at $100–$750/consumer/incident), **Colorado** (HB 24-1130 — BIPA-lite, applies from user #1 regardless of thresholds, no cure period), **Maryland** (MODPA — "strictly necessary" standard; consent is *not* a workaround; absolute ban on selling sensitive data), **New York** (SHIELD Act — security and breach duties, no consent statute *yet*).

### 🟡 Tier 3 — opt-in consent for sensitive data, AG enforcement

The remaining comprehensive-privacy states: Connecticut, Delaware, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia. Plus **Florida** (likely inapplicable — only reaches >$1B global revenue) and **Louisiana** (22nd state, May 2026).

### ⚪ Tier 4 — no biometric-specific rule

The ~28 remaining states. **You are not unregulated there** — breach-notification statutes increasingly count biometric data as personal information, and state UDAP statutes can reach a deceptive consent flow. But nothing here changes what you build.

---

## 3. State-by-state matrix

**Notation:** PRA = private right of action. "Sensitive-data opt-in" = biometrics are sensitive data under that state's comprehensive law, requiring opt-in consent + a data protection assessment.

| State | Law that binds us | Consent standard | Retention limit | PRA | Penalty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Illinois** | BIPA, 740 ILCS 14 | **Written release**, pre-capture, standalone; must state specific purpose + term. E-signature OK | Purpose satisfied **or 3 yrs** from last interaction, **whichever first**; policy must be **published** | **YES** | $1,000 negligent / $5,000 intentional, + fees |
| **Texas** | CUBI, s.503.001 | Inform + obtain consent pre-capture | ≤ **1 year** after purpose expires | No (AG only) | **$25,000/violation** |
| **Washington** | **MHMDA**, ch. 19.373 (RCW 19.375 likely N/A — excludes photos and data derived from them) | Consent for consumer health data | Reasonable | **YES (broad)** | CPA remedies |
| **Oregon (Portland)** | City ordinance | Prohibited in places of public accommodation | n/a | **YES** | **$1,000/day**, + fees |
| **California** | CCPA/CPRA + **ARL** | Sensitive-PI notice + right to limit; ARL affirmative consent | Disclosed, purpose-limited | **Breach only** ($100–$750/consumer/incident) | ~$2,663 / $7,988 intentional |
| **Colorado** | CPA + **HB 24-1130** | **Affirmative consent**; written biometric policy; applies **regardless of thresholds** | Retention limits + deletion protocols; **no sale or purchase** | No | CPA penalties; **no cure period** |
| **Maryland** | MODPA (+ MDPPA from 1 Oct 2026) | **"Strictly necessary"** — consent does not cure | Strictly necessary only | No | AG; cure sunsets 2027 |
| **New York** | SHIELD Act, GBL 899-aa/bb | — (no consent statute) | Must have retention + destruction policy | No | AG |
| **New York City** | Admin. Code 22-1201–1205 | Signage; **no profiting** | n/a | **YES** | Statutory |
| **Connecticut** | CTDPA (expanded 1 Jul 2026) | Sensitive-data opt-in | Purpose-limited | No | 60-day cure |
| **Virginia** | VCDPA (amended 1 Jul 2026) | Sensitive-data opt-in | Purpose-limited | No | 30-day cure |
| **Utah · Iowa · Tennessee · Montana · Delaware · Nebraska · New Hampshire · New Jersey · Minnesota · Oregon · Indiana · Kentucky · Rhode Island** | Comprehensive privacy law | Sensitive-data opt-in + assessment | Purpose-limited | No | AG. **No cure:** CO, RI, IN, KY |
| **Louisiana** | 22nd state, May 2026 | Consent before processing biometrics; notice if sold | — | No | AG |
| **Florida** | FDBR | Sensitive-data opt-in | — | No | **Likely N/A** (>$1B revenue only) |
| **All other ~28 states** | Breach notification; UDAP | No biometric consent rule | — | Varies | Varies |

---

## 4. The five answers you asked for

**Which laws apply?** BIPA (IL), CUBI (TX), MHMDA (WA), Portland's ordinance, plus 20+ comprehensive privacy laws treating biometrics as sensitive data. Washington's *biometric* statute probably does **not** apply, because RCW 19.375.010 excludes photographs and "data generated therefrom."

**Notice and written consent.** Only Illinois demands a signed written release with a stated purpose *and* term. But because BIPA is strictest and the cost delta is a screen and a checkbox, **build the BIPA screen for everyone.** Critically: **do not bundle** biometric consent with subscription consent or with the ToS. Bundling can fail BIPA's standalone-release requirement and California's ARL affirmative-consent requirement in one move.

**Retention.** BIPA sets the binding ceiling: purpose-satisfied or 3 years, whichever is *first*. For signup verification, "purpose satisfied" arrives in **seconds**. Texas gives a 1-year hard backstop; Maryland's "strictly necessary" is tighter still. **The defensible answer is to delete the raw scan and derived template almost immediately.**

**Private right of action.** Illinois (all violations), Washington MHMDA (broad), Portland (per-day), NYC (if it applies), California (breach only). Everywhere else: AG enforcement.

**Penalties.** $1,000/$5,000 per person (IL) · $25,000/violation (TX) · $1,000/day (Portland) · $100–$750/consumer/incident (CA breach) · $7,500/violation (WA biometric statute, if it applied).

---

## 5. The recommendation

**Build one national flow to the strictest requirement on each axis.** You do not need 50 variants:

| Axis | Strictest source | What you build |
|---|---|---|
| Consent | BIPA s.15(b) | Standalone pre-camera screen: purpose, term, e-signature |
| Retention policy | BIPA s.15(a) | Published policy page; destroy at purpose-satisfaction |
| Hard deadline | Texas CUBI | 1-year absolute backstop |
| Minimisation | Maryland MODPA | Documented necessity assessment |
| Sale | BIPA s.15(c), MODPA, CO, NYC | **Never.** Absolute product rule |
| Security | NY SHIELD + CCPA 1798.150 | Encryption at rest, breach runbook |
| Subscription | CA ARL (AB 2863) + NY 527-a | Click-to-cancel, annual reminder, 3-yr consent records |

**The one thing that most reduces risk:** choose the **ephemeral** retention model. If you never store the template, BIPA retention exposure approaches zero, Texas is trivially satisfied, Maryland's necessity test is easy, and a breach cannot leak biometrics because there are none to leak. Only choose stored templates if a named, concrete feature requires re-matching.

---

## 6. What is unresolved

Three questions need a written opinion from privacy counsel. They are captured in their own task:

1. **Washington** — is an identity-only face scan "consumer health data" under MHMDA? *Biggest open question in this research.* MHMDA has a broad private right of action.
2. **Portland** — is a mobile app a "place of public accommodation"? The device-verification exception appears to cover unlocking a device, not verifying a user, so do not rely on it.
3. **NYC** — is a mobile app a "commercial establishment"? Reads as physical premises, but the ordinance carries a PRA.

## 7. Moving targets — check quarterly

- **Massachusetts and New York** both have pending BIPA-style bills that would create **private rights of action**. If New York passes one, the risk map changes materially.
- **Maryland** MDPPA of 2026 effective 1 Oct 2026.
- **FTC** negative-option rulemaking restarted after the Eighth Circuit vacatur; comments closed 13 April 2026.
- **Colorado AI Act** replacement (SB 26-189) effective 1 Jan 2027 — significantly narrowed; roadmap item, not a launch blocker.

---

## 8. Coverage note

The matrix names every state, but the depth is deliberately uneven. I researched the ~20 states with rules that change your product decisions in real detail. For the remaining ~28, I verified that no biometric-specific consent statute exists rather than auditing each state's UDAP and breach-notification law line by line. That is the right allocation of effort for a launch decision, but it is a *scoping choice* and you should know I made it.

subtasks.title: Tier 1: Illinois BIPA — consent mechanics, retention, damages, per-scan accrual
subtasks.description:
Illinois BIPA, 740 ILCS 14 — RESEARCHED.

APPLIES TO US: yes, unambiguously. A "scan of face geometry" is an enumerated biometric identifier. No revenue/size threshold — BIPA applies to any "private entity" collecting from an Illinois resident.

WHAT S.15 REQUIRES (all four, and 15(a)+15(b) are the ones that get sued):
- 15(a) Maintain a WRITTEN, PUBLICLY AVAILABLE retention + destruction policy. Must destroy when the initial purpose is satisfied OR within 3 years of the individual's last interaction, WHICHEVER IS FIRST. For us, "purpose satisfied" = the moment identity verification completes, so our defensible retention of the raw scan/template is measured in seconds-to-days, not years. Publishing the policy is a separate obligation from following it — publish it in the app and on the website.
- 15(b) Before capture: inform in writing that biometrics are being collected/stored; inform in writing of the SPECIFIC PURPOSE and the SPECIFIC TERM of collection/storage; and obtain a signed WRITTEN RELEASE. SB 2979 (Aug 2024) confirmed electronic signature satisfies "written release" — so an in-app e-signature/checkbox flow is valid if it's a standalone affirmative act.
- 15(c) No selling, leasing, trading, or otherwise PROFITING from biometric data. Flat ban, no consent exception. Relevant if we ever monetise the verification data or share it with an ad/analytics partner.
- 15(d) No disclosure/redisclosure without separate consent. This catches our identity-verification VENDOR if data flows to them — need consent language naming the vendor.

LIABILITY:
- Private right of action, s.20. Statutory damages: $1,000 per negligent violation, $5,000 per intentional/reckless, whichever is greater than actual damages, PLUS attorneys' fees and costs and injunctive relief.
- Rosenbach v. Six Flags (2019 IL 123186): no actual injury needed. A bare notice-and-consent violation makes you "aggrieved" and gives standing. This is why BIPA is a class-action engine.
- Tims v. Black Horse Carriers (2023): uniform 5-year statute of limitations for all BIPA claims.
- Cothron v. White Castle (2023) held every separate capture was a separate violation. SB 2979 / P.A. 103-0769 (eff. 2 Aug 2024) REVERSED this for 15(b) and 15(d): now a single recovery per person per type of violation, regardless of how many times the same method collected data. Retroactivity has been litigated and at least one federal court has applied it retroactively.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR OUR MATH: SB 2979 caps the per-user exposure but does NOT reduce per-class exposure. A 100,000-Illinois-user class at $1,000/person negligent = $100M nominal. The amendment changed BIPA from existential to merely severe. Illinois remains the highest-risk state in the country for this product.

subtasks.title: Tier 1: Texas CUBI + Washington HB 1493 — the two AG-enforced biometric statutes
subtasks.description:
TEXAS CUBI + WASHINGTON — RESEARCHED. Key finding: the real Washington risk is NOT the biometric statute.

=== TEXAS: CUBI, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code s.503.001 ===
APPLIES: yes. "Biometric identifier" expressly includes a "record of hand or face geometry."
REQUIREMENTS: before capturing for a commercial purpose you must (1) INFORM the individual and (2) RECEIVE CONSENT. Notably the statute does not on its face require the consent to be written — but do it in writing anyway; there is no reason to litigate this.
RETENTION: must destroy within a reasonable time, and not later than 1 YEAR after the purpose for collection expires.
NO SALE: cannot sell/lease/disclose except in narrow exceptions.
PENALTY: civil penalty up to $25,000 PER VIOLATION. No private right of action — the Texas AG has EXCLUSIVE enforcement authority.
WHY TEXAS IS ACTUALLY DANGEROUS DESPITE HAVING NO PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: the AG has taken the position that unlawful collection AND continued storage are SEPARATE violations, so a single bad collection can be $50,000. The AG obtained a $1.4 BILLION settlement from Meta over face-tagging — described by that office as the largest ever obtained by a single state — and a separate settlement from Google. This is an office that actively hunts face-scanning products.
2026 CHANGE: TRAIGA (HB 149), effective 1 Jan 2026, amended CUBI. Three points: (a) publicly available photos/recordings do NOT constitute consent unless the individual themselves made the content public; (b) processing biometrics solely to develop/train/evaluate an AI model is exempt UNLESS the resulting system is used to uniquely identify a specific individual — our product IS used to uniquely identify, so THIS EXEMPTION DOES NOT HELP US; (c) TRAIGA enforcement carries AG notice and a 60-day cure period.

=== WASHINGTON: two separate laws, and the obvious one probably doesn't apply ===
(1) RCW 19.375 (HB 1493) — LIKELY DOES NOT COVER US. RCW 19.375.010 excludes from "biometric identifier" a "physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording or data generated therefrom." A face scan derived from the phone camera is strongly arguable to be "data generated therefrom" and thus outside the statute. Also: AG-exclusive enforcement under the Consumer Protection Act (RCW 19.86), up to $7,500 per violation, NO private right of action. Requires notice + consent before ENROLLING in a database for a commercial purpose; retention no longer than reasonably necessary.
(2) MY HEALTH MY DATA ACT, ch. 19.373 RCW — THIS IS THE WASHINGTON RISK. Broad definition of "consumer health data" that reaches well beyond ordinary health information and enumerates biometric data. Critically it carries a BROAD PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION via the Consumer Protection Act, with plaintiff-friendly presumptions. No specified statutory damages, so plaintiffs must plead actual damages — but CPA treble damages and fees are available.
UNRESOLVED / NEEDS COUNSEL: whether a face scan used purely for identity verification (not to infer any health condition) is "consumer health data" under MHMDA. There is a real argument it is not, because it says nothing about health status. This is not settled and it is the single biggest open legal question in this research. Do not launch in WA assuming the answer is no without a written opinion.
Washington has NO comprehensive consumer privacy law as of 2026.

subtasks.title: Tier 2: Which comprehensive state privacy laws are in force, and what they require for biometric sensitive data
subtasks.description:
COMPREHENSIVE STATE PRIVACY LAWS — RESEARCHED.

THE LIST (20 states with comprehensive laws in force as of Aug 2026): California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida (narrow), Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia. Newest three — Indiana (SB 5), Kentucky (HB 15), Rhode Island (HB 7787/SB 2500) — all effective 1 Jan 2026. Florida's Digital Bill of Rights only reaches companies with >$1B global revenue, so it likely does NOT apply to us at launch.

THE COMMON RULE THAT BINDS US: every one of these treats biometric data as SENSITIVE DATA, and in nearly all of them processing sensitive data requires OPT-IN CONSENT. Plus: a data protection assessment / risk assessment for sensitive-data processing, honouring universal opt-out signals, and the standard six rights (access, delete, correct, portability, opt-out, non-discrimination).

PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: California is the ONLY comprehensive-law state with one, and it is narrow — Cal. Civ. Code s.1798.150 covers data BREACH only, not consent failures. Statutory damages $100–$750 per consumer per incident or actual damages if higher. Consumer must give 30 days' written notice and the business can cure. Our face templates are exactly the kind of data that makes a breach class action expensive, so encryption at rest is a legal control, not just a security one.
Other CA enforcement: AG and CPPA, with penalties around $2,663 per violation and $7,988 per intentional violation.

THE THREE STATES THAT GO FURTHER THAN "OPT-IN CONSENT":

1. MARYLAND (MODPA) — THE STRICTEST STATE FOR OUR DATA. Sensitive data may only be collected/processed/shared where STRICTLY NECESSARY to provide the product the consumer requested. Consent is NOT a workaround. Blanket prohibition on SELLING sensitive data — first of its kind, and consent does not override it. Effective Oct 2025, enforceable Apr 2026, cure period sunsets 2027. Practical effect: we must be able to document a necessity assessment showing the face scan is strictly necessary for signup identity verification, and we can never monetise it.

2. COLORADO (CPA as amended by HB 24-1130, eff. 1 Jul 2025) — a BIPA-lite bolted onto a comprehensive law. Requires affirmative consent for biometric identifiers, a written biometric policy, retention limits and deletion protocols, and prohibits sale AND purchase of biometric identifiers (C.R.S. 6-1-1301 et seq.). CRITICALLY: the biometric provisions apply regardless of the CPA's usual applicability thresholds, so we are covered in Colorado from user #1. Also covers employees. Colorado has NO cure period. SB 24-041 (eff. Oct 2025) adds minors' protections including parental consent under 13.

3. Cure periods generally: Colorado and Rhode Island have none. Indiana and Kentucky removed theirs before their laws took effect. Virginia 30 days, Connecticut 60. The trend is away from free first bites.

2026 AMENDMENT WATCH: Connecticut's expanded CTDPA mostly took effect 1 Jul 2026; Virginia and Connecticut now ban sale of precise geolocation (joining Maryland and Oregon); Maryland, New Hampshire and New Jersey also saw changes. Four more states adopted comprehensive laws in mid-2026 that are not yet effective — these need a re-check before launch, see the human subtask.

subtasks.title: Tier 3: City and sector rules that catch face scans (NYC, Portland, Baltimore, CO AI Act)
subtasks.description:
CITY / SECTOR / ADJACENT RULES — RESEARCHED. Headline: the two scariest-looking local laws probably don't reach a mobile app, but "probably" is doing work and both need a counsel sign-off.

1. NEW YORK CITY — Admin. Code ss.22-1201 to 22-1205 (eff. July 2021). HAS A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION for "aggrieved" persons, which is the BIPA fact pattern that generated the class-action wave. TWO duties: (a) clear and conspicuous plain-language SIGNAGE where biometric identifier information is collected; (b) a blanket ban on selling, sharing or otherwise profiting from BII.
LIKELY DOES NOT APPLY TO US: the signage duty attaches to "COMMERCIAL ESTABLISHMENTS," defined as places of entertainment, retail stores, and food and drink establishments — i.e. physical premises. A mobile app is not obviously any of those. ACTION: get this confirmed in writing; if we ever open a physical presence or kiosk in NYC, the signage duty switches on immediately.

2. PORTLAND, OREGON — city ordinance eff. 1 Jan 2021, the first US jurisdiction to ban PRIVATE use of face recognition. PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION with statutory damages of $1,000 PER DAY of violation (or actual damages if greater) plus attorneys' fees.
SCOPE: bans use by private entities in "places of public accommodation" within Portland, excluding places distinctly private. Exceptions include compliance with law and an individual using FRT to verify access to a personal or employer-issued device.
WHY THIS IS THE MOST UNDER-RATED ITEM IN THE RESEARCH: the per-day damages structure means exposure scales with TIME, not with number of users — a long-running violation is expensive even with few Portland users. Whether a consumer app is a "place of public accommodation" is genuinely unsettled. The device-verification exception is about unlocking a device, NOT about a service verifying who you are, so do not rely on it. ACTION: counsel opinion before enabling signup for Portland users.

3. COLORADO AI ACT — NOT A LAUNCH BLOCKER. Original SB 24-205 was delayed from Feb 2026 to 30 Jun 2026, then on 14 May 2026 Governor Polis signed SB 26-189, which REPLACES it with a narrower transparency/disclosure framework and pushes the effective date to 1 JAN 2027. The new law strips out the duty of care on algorithmic discrimination, the deployer risk-management programs and the impact assessments. Put a roadmap item on this for H2 2027, not for launch.

4. NEW YORK STATE — SHIELD Act, GBL ss.899-aa and 899-bb. New York has NO biometric consent statute, but the SHIELD Act (a) puts biometric information inside the definition of "private information" for BREACH NOTIFICATION, and (b) imposes an affirmative REASONABLE SECURITY requirement including data retention and destruction policies. It reaches any entity holding biometric data of New York residents even with no operations in the state. GBL 899-aa was amended in Dec 2024. So New York does bind us — just on security and breach response rather than on consent.

5. GENERAL BREACH-NOTIFICATION POINT: a growing set of states now count biometric data as "personal information" triggering breach notification. Treat the face template as notifiable data everywhere and build the incident-response runbook once, nationally.

6. BALTIMORE — its private-sector face recognition ordinance carried a sunset provision and is not currently a live constraint; re-check only if we plan a physical presence there.

subtasks.title: Subscription exposure: FTC click-to-cancel status + California and NY auto-renewal law
subtasks.description:
SUBSCRIPTION / AUTO-RENEWAL EXPOSURE — RESEARCHED. Not in the original brief but triggered directly by the monthly subscription. This is a second, independent class-action surface layered on top of the biometric one.

FEDERAL — the rule is gone, the enforcement is not:
- The FTC's Negative Option / "Click-to-Cancel" Rule was VACATED IN ITS ENTIRETY by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025, on procedural Magnuson-Moss grounds — not because the substance was wrong.
- The FTC has RESTARTED the rulemaking with an ANPRM; comments were due 13 April 2026. A replacement rule is in flux and could land during our first year of operation.
- ROSCA and FTC Act s.5 still apply and the FTC continues to enforce. The FTC's interpretation of ROSCA is that cancellation must be AT LEAST AS EASY as the method used to sign up. State AGs are also active here.
- PRACTICAL CONCLUSION: build to the vacated rule's standard anyway. It is the likely shape of the replacement, it is already state law in California, and there is no commercial upside to a hard cancellation flow.

CALIFORNIA ARL — Bus. & Prof. Code s.17600 et seq., as amended by AB 2863, in effect since 1 JULY 2025. The strictest in the country and effectively our national baseline:
- Free trials / "free-to-pay conversions" are expressly inside the definition of automatic renewal and continuous service.
- Clear and conspicuous disclosure of material terms BEFORE consent; separate affirmative consent to the auto-renewal terms specifically.
- CLICK-TO-CANCEL: cancellation must be available through the SAME CHANNEL used to sign up, with an online cancel button, and the business cannot obstruct or delay cancellation.
- ANNUAL REMINDER to the consumer: renewal frequency, amount charged, and clear cancellation instructions.
- RECORDKEEPING: retain proof of the consumer's affirmative consent for at least 3 YEARS, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer. This is an engineering requirement — log and retain the consent artifact, not just the consent flag.
- LIABILITY MECHANICS: s.17603 deems goods/services supplied without proper affirmative consent an "UNCONDITIONAL GIFT" the consumer need not pay for. Courts (Mayron v. Google) have held the ARL has NO standalone private right of action and that the unconditional-gift provision is a shield, not a sword — but plaintiffs routinely plead ARL violations THROUGH the UCL (s.17200) and CLRA, and can get there by alleging they would not have subscribed, or would have cancelled, absent the violation. Treat this as a live class-action risk, just one with a pleading hurdle.

NEW YORK — GBL s.527-a. Clear and conspicuous presentation of material terms before consent: description, cost, frequency of charges, the deadline to act to stop further charges, and the cancellation mechanism. Advance notice of material changes including price increases, at least 5 business days and no more than 30 days before the change. Cancellation mechanism requirements and a refund pathway where a consumer cancels within at least fourteen days of a charge.

OTHER STATES: most states now have some auto-renewal statute. Because California's is the strictest on consent, cancellation and recordkeeping, and New York adds the price-change notice, building to CA + NY together gets us substantially to national compliance. Confirm the residual states with counsel rather than researching 50 separately — the marginal requirements are small.

subtasks.title: Synthesize the 50-state matrix and rank launch risk
subtasks.description:
SYNTHESIS COMPLETE — see the report attached to the parent task for the full 50-state matrix and risk ranking.

THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL OUTPUT: build ONE national compliance flow to the strictest-in-class requirement on each axis, rather than 50 variants. The strictest source on each axis is:
- Notice + written release, pre-capture, standalone: ILLINOIS BIPA s.15(b)
- Published retention/destruction policy: ILLINOIS BIPA s.15(a) — destroy at purpose-satisfaction or 3 years, whichever first
- Hard outer retention deadline: TEXAS CUBI — 1 year after purpose expires (BIPA's "purpose satisfied" prong is tighter in practice)
- Data minimisation standard: MARYLAND MODPA — "strictly necessary," consent is not a workaround
- Never sell / never profit: BIPA s.15(c), MODPA, Colorado, NYC — treat as an absolute product rule
- Security + breach: NY SHIELD Act reasonable security; CCPA s.1798.150 makes a breach of this data privately actionable
- Subscription consent + cancellation + recordkeeping: CALIFORNIA ARL as amended by AB 2863, plus NY GBL s.527-a price-change notice

FORWARD-RISK ITEMS FOUND DURING SYNTHESIS (not launch blockers, but they will move):
- LOUISIANA became the 22nd comprehensive-privacy state in May 2026; requires consent before processing biometrics and a conspicuous notice if biometric data is sold.
- MARYLAND Data Privacy and Protection Act of 2026 (HB0264) takes effect 1 Oct 2026 — addresses biometric identifiers, collection/retention limits, deletion or de-identification, privacy notices. Maryland is stacking obligations.
- MASSACHUSETTS and NEW YORK both have pending BIPA-style bills that WOULD CREATE PRIVATE RIGHTS OF ACTION. If either passes, the risk map changes materially — NY especially, given population. This is the thing to monitor quarterly.
- Colorado AI Act replacement (SB 26-189) effective 1 Jan 2027.
- FTC negative-option replacement rule in active rulemaking.

subtasks.title: DECISION: pick the retention model — ephemeral template vs. stored template
subtasks.description:
This is the single highest-leverage product decision in the whole compliance picture and only you can make it.

OPTION A — EPHEMERAL: capture the face scan, run the match, delete the raw image AND the derived template within seconds, persist only a boolean 'verified' flag plus an audit record with no biometric content. This collapses risk almost everywhere: BIPA s.15(a) retention exposure goes to near zero, Texas CUBI's 1-year deadline is trivially met, Maryland's 'strictly necessary' test is easy to pass, and a data breach cannot leak face templates because there are none.

OPTION B — STORED TEMPLATE: keep the template to support re-verification, fraud detection, or account recovery. Every requirement in the report gets harder, and a breach becomes a CCPA s.1798.150 class action at $100-$750 per California consumer per incident.

If the product does not have a concrete, named feature that requires re-matching against a stored template, choose A. Most identity-verification-at-signup products do not. Whichever you choose, the answer determines the retention language that must appear in the BIPA-compliant consent screen, so this has to be decided before the consent copy is written.

subtasks.title: DECISION: geofence Illinois, Texas and Portland at launch, or comply everywhere from day one?
subtasks.description:
Two viable strategies. Pick one before engineering builds the signup flow.

STRATEGY 1 — COMPLY NATIONALLY FROM DAY ONE. Build the BIPA-grade consent flow for every user regardless of state. Higher upfront cost, no geo logic, no risk of a geofence leaking. This is the right answer if identity verification is core to the product.

STRATEGY 2 — STAGED LAUNCH. Block signup from Illinois (and consider Portland OR) until the compliance flow is legally reviewed, then switch them on. Note that geofencing is imperfect — VPNs, travellers and billing-address mismatches all create users you thought you excluded, and BIPA applies to Illinois residents rather than to people physically in Illinois. A leaky geofence is arguably worse than no geofence because it looks like you knew the law applied and tried to dodge it.

RECOMMENDATION: Strategy 1. The delta in build cost between a compliant consent flow and a non-compliant one is small — it is mostly screen copy, a checkbox, a published policy page and a deletion job. The delta in risk is enormous.

subtasks.title: Engage privacy counsel on the three unresolved legal questions
subtasks.description:
Three questions came out of the research that genuinely cannot be resolved without a licensed attorney giving a written opinion. Send these three, exactly as written, to privacy counsel. Do not let this become a general 'review our compliance' engagement — these are the specific questions.

Q1 — WASHINGTON: Is a face scan collected solely for identity verification, from which no health inference is drawn, 'consumer health data' under the My Health My Data Act (ch. 19.373 RCW)? MHMDA has a broad private right of action via the Consumer Protection Act with plaintiff-friendly presumptions. Note that RCW 19.375 (the biometric statute) likely does NOT apply because RCW 19.375.010 excludes photographs and 'data generated therefrom'. This is the biggest open question in the research.

Q2 — PORTLAND, OREGON: Is a consumer mobile app a 'place of public accommodation' under the Portland private-sector face recognition ban? Statutory damages are $1,000 PER DAY plus attorneys' fees, and there is a private right of action, so exposure scales with elapsed time rather than user count. The ordinance's device-verification exception appears to cover unlocking a device, not a service verifying a user's identity — please confirm.

Q3 — NEW YORK CITY: Is a mobile app a 'commercial establishment' under NYC Admin. Code ss.22-1201 to 22-1205? The definition reaches places of entertainment, retail stores and food and drink establishments, which reads as physical premises — but the ordinance carries a private right of action, so a wrong answer is expensive.

Ask counsel to confirm in writing and to flag whether the BIPA SB 2979 retroactivity question affects any pre-launch data we may already hold.

subtasks.title: Write the BIPA-grade consent screen copy and get it legally reviewed
subtasks.description:
One screen, shown BEFORE the camera activates, that satisfies the strictest state simultaneously. It must contain all of the following or it fails BIPA s.15(b):

1. A written statement that biometric identifiers are being COLLECTED AND STORED.
2. The SPECIFIC PURPOSE, stated narrowly — e.g. 'to verify your identity when you create your account.' Do not write 'to improve our services'; a broad purpose defeats Maryland's 'strictly necessary' test and undercuts the retention argument.
3. The SPECIFIC TERM of collection and storage — an actual duration, matching whatever was decided in the retention-model task.
4. A STANDALONE affirmative action constituting a written release. Not bundled into the general Terms of Service acceptance. Electronic signature is valid under BIPA post-SB 2979.
5. Named disclosure to any third-party identity-verification VENDOR, to satisfy BIPA s.15(d) and the equivalent consent requirements elsewhere.
6. A separate, clearly distinct consent for the auto-renewing subscription — do NOT bundle biometric consent and subscription consent into one checkbox. Bundling risks failing both BIPA's standalone-release requirement and the California ARL's affirmative-consent requirement in a single stroke.

Deliverable: final copy, reviewed by counsel, ready to hand to design.

subtasks.title: Publish the written biometric retention and destruction policy
subtasks.description:
BIPA s.15(a) requires a WRITTEN policy, MADE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC, establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanent destruction. Colorado's HB 24-1130 independently requires a biometric policy. Publishing it is a separate legal obligation from following it — companies get sued for having good practices and no published policy.

Must state: what biometric data is collected; the retention period; the destruction trigger (purpose satisfied, or 3 years from last interaction, whichever is FIRST — BIPA s.15(a)); and the destruction method.

Must be genuinely public: linked from the app, the website footer, and the privacy policy. Not buried inside the Terms of Service.

Also confirm the Texas backstop is satisfied: CUBI requires destruction within a reasonable time and no later than 1 year after the purpose expires.

subtasks.title: Build the automated deletion job and prove it actually runs
subtasks.description:
A published retention policy that the system does not enforce is worse than no policy — it is documentary evidence of the violation. Engineering task:

1. Automated deletion of raw face images and derived templates on the schedule stated in the published policy.
2. Logged proof of deletion, retained as an audit artifact (the audit log itself must contain no biometric content).
3. A test that fails CI if records exceed the retention window.
4. Encryption at rest for any biometric data that does persist — this is a legal control, not just a security one, because CCPA s.1798.150 gives a private right of action with $100-$750 per consumer per incident for breaches of unencrypted data, and the NY SHIELD Act imposes an affirmative reasonable-security duty on holders of biometric data of NY residents.
5. Wire deletion into the consumer deletion-rights flow required by all 20+ comprehensive-privacy states.

subtasks.title: Build the subscription flow to California ARL + NY GBL 527-a standard
subtasks.description:
Separate workstream from the biometric one, same launch deadline. Build to California's Automatic Renewal Law as amended by AB 2863 (in effect since 1 July 2025) because it is the strictest, and add New York's price-change notice.

CHECKLIST:
- Clear and conspicuous disclosure of all material terms BEFORE consent: what the service is, the amount, the charge frequency, the deadline to act to stop charges, and how to cancel.
- Separate affirmative consent to the auto-renewal terms specifically — not bundled with the biometric consent, not bundled with the ToS.
- CLICK-TO-CANCEL: cancellation available in the SAME CHANNEL used to sign up, online cancel button, no obstruction or delay, no retention-offer maze.
- Annual reminder: renewal frequency, amount charged, cancellation instructions.
- Any free trial is a 'free-to-pay conversion' and is fully inside the ARL.
- RECORDKEEPING (engineering): retain the consent artifact for at least 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer.
- NY GBL s.527-a: notice of material changes including price increases, at least 5 business days and no more than 30 days before the change.

CONTEXT: the FTC click-to-cancel rule was vacated by the Eighth Circuit in July 2025 and a replacement is in active rulemaking, but ROSCA and FTC Act s.5 enforcement continue and the FTC reads ROSCA to require cancellation at least as easy as signup. Build to the strict standard regardless.

subtasks.title: Set a quarterly recurring check on the four moving legal targets
subtasks.description:
This area is changing faster than an annual review can track. Diary a quarterly 30-minute check on:

1. MASSACHUSETTS and NEW YORK BIPA-style bills — both had proposals in early 2026 that would create PRIVATE RIGHTS OF ACTION for biometric violations. If either passes, the national risk map changes materially and NY in particular would become a Tier 1 danger state.
2. LOUISIANA — became the 22nd comprehensive-privacy state in May 2026; requires consent before processing biometrics and conspicuous notice if biometric data is sold. Confirm the effective date and fold into the matrix.
3. MARYLAND Data Privacy and Protection Act of 2026 (HB0264), effective 1 Oct 2026 — further biometric collection/retention limits and deletion or de-identification duties on top of MODPA.
4. FTC negative-option rulemaking — ANPRM comments closed 13 April 2026; a replacement click-to-cancel rule could land mid-operation. Also watch the Colorado AI Act replacement (SB 26-189), effective 1 Jan 2027.
